question: How is a PWC propelled and steered?
choice_a: By a traditional rudder mounted at the stern
choice_b: Water is drawn into a pump and forced out under pressure through a steering nozzle, directed by the steering control
choice_c: By twin propellers on either side of the hull
choice_d: By an outboard motor that pivots independently of the handlebars
explanation: A PWC is propelled by drawing water into a pump and forcing it out under pressure through a steering nozzle; turning the steering control turns the nozzle in the same direction.

question: What happens to steering control on most PWC if the engine returns to idle or shuts off during operation?
choice_a: Nothing changes; steering is independent of engine power
choice_c: The operator may lose all steering control
explanation: Most PWC and other jet-drive vessels must have power to maintain control; if the engine returns to idle or shuts off, the operator may lose all steering control, though newer PWC allow for off-throttle steering.

question: Do most PWC have brakes?
choice_a: Braking is optional equipment on all models
choice_b: Yes, all PWC are required to have hydraulic brakes
choice_c: Yes, but only models built after 2020
choice_d: No, most PWC do not have brakes, so plenty of room for stopping must be allowed
explanation: Most PWC do not have brakes; releasing the throttle or shutting off the engine does not mean the PWC will stop immediately, even on models with a braking system.

question: After capsizing a PWC, how do most riders know which direction to roll it back upright?
choice_a: A decal placed by the manufacturer at the rear or bottom of the craft indicates the roll direction
choice_c: There is a universal rule to always roll left
choice_d: The owner's manual never covers this topic
explanation: Most manufacturers place a decal at the rear or bottom of the craft indicating the direction to roll the PWC to return it upright; if no decal exists, check the owner's manual or ask the dealer.

question: Why does the Guide recommend avoiding PWC operation when very tired?
choice_b: Because reboarding after a fall would be difficult
choice_c: Because tired riders use more fuel
choice_d: There is no such recommendation in the Guide
explanation: The Guide recommends not riding a PWC if very tired because reboarding would be difficult, and to avoid strong currents or winds that could hamper reboarding efforts.

question: According to the Guide's courtesy tips, what should a PWC operator do to reduce annoying noise near shore?
choice_b: Operate at the highest possible RPM at all times
choice_c: Vary the operating area and avoid congregating with other PWC operators near shore
choice_d: Modify the exhaust system to reduce sound
explanation: Courteous PWC operation includes varying the operating area, not repeating the same maneuver, and avoiding congregating with other PWC operators near shore, which increases noise levels.

question: Why does the Guide caution against modifying a PWC's exhaust system?
choice_b: It is illegal only if done by a non-dealer
choice_c: Modified exhausts are always faster and quieter
choice_d: An improperly modified exhaust will not make the PWC faster and may raise noise to an illegal level
explanation: Improperly modified exhaust systems will not make a PWC faster and may raise the noise level to an illegal level.

question: According to the Guide's environmental guidance, how deep should the water be before operating a PWC, to avoid damaging bottom sediment or vegetation?
choice_d: Depth does not matter for PWC
explanation: Operators should make sure the water they operate in is at least 24 inches deep; riding in shallow water can cause bottom sediments or aquatic vegetation to be sucked into the pump.

question: Before cleaning debris from a PWC's pump intake area, what must the operator do first?
choice_a: Increase throttle to clear it automatically
explanation: Keep hands, feet, loose clothing, and hair away from the pump intake area; before cleaning debris away from the pump intake, be sure to shut off the engine.

question: May a child under 7 years of age ride on or be towed behind a PWC in Michigan?
choice_c: Only with a parent or guardian, or a designee of the parent or guardian
explanation: You may not allow a child under 7 years of age to ride on or be towed behind a PWC unless with a parent or guardian or a designee of the parent or guardian.

question: During what hours is it illegal to operate a PWC in Michigan?
choice_a: PWC may be operated at any hour
explanation: It is illegal to operate a PWC during the period that begins at sunset and ends at 8:00 a.m., with 'sunset' determined by the National Weather Service.

question: At what speed must a PWC be operated if crossing within 150 feet behind another vessel (that is not also a PWC)?
choice_d: There is no speed restriction for crossing behind another vessel
explanation: A PWC must be operated at 'slow, no wake speed' if crossing within 150 feet behind another vessel unless the other vessel is also a PWC.

question: How close to a Great Lakes shoreline may a PWC operate above slow-no-wake speed?
choice_a: There is no shoreline distance restriction for PWC
choice_b: A PWC may not operate within 200 feet of a Great Lakes shoreline unless at slow, no wake speed and perpendicular to shore
choice_c: PWC must stay at least 500 feet from any shoreline at all times
explanation: You may not operate a PWC within 200 feet of a Great Lakes shoreline unless traveling at slow, no wake speed perpendicular to the shoreline.

question: In which national park areas are PWC prohibited within the boundaries?
choice_c: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore and Isle Royale National Park
explanation: PWC are prohibited within the boundaries of Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore and Isle Royale National Park, with additional restrictions at Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore.

question: Everyone being towed on water skis, a surfboard, or a similar device must wear what kind of PFD?
choice_a: A Type IV throwable cushion only
choice_c: No PFD is required if the tow rope has a quick-release
choice_d: A USCG-approved wearable PFD; inflatable PFDs are not allowed
explanation: Everyone being towed behind a vessel on water skis, a surfboard, or similar device must wear a USCG-approved wearable PFD; inflatable PFDs are not allowed.

question: When towing a person on water skis, what additional crew member must be aboard the towing vessel besides the operator?
choice_a: A person observing the towed person(s) at all times
choice_c: No additional crew member is required if a wide-angle mirror is installed
explanation: Every vessel towing a person on water skis, a surfboard, or a similar device must have a person on board, in addition to the operator, observing the towed person at all times.

question: During what hours may a person be legally towed on water skis behind a PWC?
choice_a: Sunrise to sunset with no time restriction
choice_c: One hour before sunrise to one hour after sunset
choice_d: Any time of day or night
explanation: It is legal to tow persons on water skis behind a PWC only between 8:00 a.m. and sunset (versus one hour before sunrise to one hour after sunset if towed behind a boat).

question: Persons being towed on water skis must stay at least how far from a dock or raft?
explanation: Persons being towed must stay at least 100 feet away from a shoreline (in water less than three feet deep), any moored or anchored vessel, a dock or raft, or any marked swimming area or person in the water.
